title: Leviathan Slain and the Vineyard Restored
summary: The LORD will slay Leviathan, the fleeing and coiling serpent, the dragon of the sea. A new song celebrates the vineyard the LORD guards, and Israel will take root and fill the world with fruit. Israel's punishment has been measured, meant to purge her idolatry, while the proud city lies abandoned; in the end the great ram's horn will sound and the scattered exiles will come home to worship on the holy mountain.
story: This chapter closes the section of chapters 24 to 27. It began with the earth laid waste and ends with Israel's exiles gathered to Jerusalem, so the whole section moves from universal judgment to worship. Two older pictures return transformed. The serpent of the sea, the ancient image of chaos, is finally killed. And the vineyard of 5:1-7, which the LORD had abandoned to thorns because it produced only bad grapes, is now tended night and day and fills the world with fruit. After this, the book returns in chapter 28 to the concrete politics of Isaiah's own day, the drunken leaders of Samaria and Jerusalem.
historical:
The dating of this chapter follows the wider debate over chapters 24 to 27. On the traditional view Isaiah wrote it in the Assyrian period, and the mention of exiles in Assyria and Egypt (verse 13) fits the deportations Assyria carried out from the northern kingdom, especially after the fall of Samaria in 722 BC, and the Israelites who fled to Egypt. On a later dating it reflects the scattered Jewish communities of the Persian period, when there were Jews in Mesopotamia and in Egypt (for example the Jewish garrison at Elephantine on the Nile in the fifth century BC). The borders in verse 12, from the Euphrates to the Wadi of Egypt, are the ideal borders of the land promised to Abraham (Genesis 15:18), not the borders Judah actually held in either period.

The unnamed fortified city of verse 10 is again difficult to identify. Some take it as the oppressor's city, others as Samaria or Jerusalem under judgment, since verse 11 speaks of a people without understanding on whom their Maker has no compassion. The context of verses 7 to 11, which deal with Israel's own punishment, makes an Israelite city plausible, but interpreters remain divided.
cultural:
Leviathan was not invented by Israel. Clay tablets found at Ugarit, a city on the Syrian coast destroyed around 1200 BC, tell how the storm god Baal defeated a sea monster called Lotan, described with the same phrases Isaiah uses: the fleeing serpent and the twisting serpent, with seven heads. Israel's poets used that well-known figure to speak of the forces of chaos and of the enemy powers behind the nations (compare Psalm 74:13-14). Isaiah does not treat Leviathan as a rival god; the LORD simply kills it with his sword, and the whole battle takes one verse.

Other details come from daily life. Asherah poles were wooden cult objects associated with the goddess Asherah, often set up beside altars at local shrines; destroying them was the mark of genuine reform (2 Kings 18:4). Crushing altar stones to chalk meant that no shrine could be rebuilt from them. Threshing (verse 12) separated grain from stalks by beating, and gleaning grain one by one describes a careful harvest where nothing is lost. The shofar, a ram's horn, was blown to call assemblies, sound alarms, and announce holy days; its blast here summons the scattered people home.
literary: The chapter is built from four units, several beginning with the phrase "in that day" (verses 1, 2, 12, and 13). Verse 1 is a brief mythic battle. Verses 2 to 6 are a vineyard song that answers the vineyard song of 5:1-7: there the owner asked what more he could have done and then removed its hedge; here he says "I am not angry," guards it continually, and invites even his enemies, the thorns and briers, to make peace with him. Verses 7 to 11 are a meditation on the difference between God's discipline of Israel and his judgment of her oppressors. Verses 12 and 13 close with two parallel promises of gathering, one by threshing and one by trumpet. The phrase "let them make peace with Me" is repeated in verse 5 for emphasis, a rare invitation in the middle of a warning.

outline.t: The LORD slays Leviathan, the serpent of the sea
The song of the fruitful vineyard
Israel's measured punishment and the deserted city
The great gathering at the sound of the ram's horn

doctrines.note: The chaos powers that ancient peoples feared are no match for the LORD. He kills Leviathan with a sword; there is no cosmic struggle between equals. Every power in creation, however monstrous, is subject to him.
Verse 9 says Jacob's guilt will be atoned for, and the evidence will be the crushing of altar stones and the removal of Asherah poles. Forgiveness and the forsaking of idols belong together.

God's discipline of Israel is measured and purposeful (verses 7 and 8), unlike his judgment on her oppressors. He keeps his vineyard and gathers his scattered people, faithful to his promises to Jacob.

words.note: Liwyatan, Leviathan. In Job 41 the word names a fearsome sea creature beyond human control, and in Psalm 74:14 a many-headed monster God crushed. Here it stands for the chaotic powers behind the world's hostility to God. Its defeat signals that God's rule will be complete.

Kipper, to atone, to make atonement. The word is used for the removal of sin and its consequences, most often through sacrifice. In verse 9 Jacob's guilt is atoned for, and the fruit of that removal is a people who dismantle their idols. Atonement is God's gift, and it changes the one who receives it.

Shofar, the ram's horn. It announced the Day of Atonement in the Year of Jubilee (Leviticus 25:9), gathered troops, and sounded alarms. In verse 13 the great shofar summons the perishing and the exiles to worship in Jerusalem, a sound of release and homecoming.

christ: Two images in this chapter return in the New Testament. Revelation identifies the great dragon as the ancient serpent, the devil and Satan (Revelation 12:9), and describes his final defeat, drawing on the Leviathan tradition of verse 1 alongside the serpent of Genesis 3. The link is thematic: Isaiah pictures God's victory over chaos, and the New Testament locates that victory in Christ's death and resurrection. The vineyard also returns. Jesus told a parable of a vineyard whose tenants rejected the owner's son (Mark 12:1-12), built on Isaiah 5, and in John 15 he calls himself the true vine, whose branches bear fruit. The promise that Israel would fill the world with fruit is taken up in the gospel going to the nations. And the great trumpet that gathers God's scattered people appears in Jesus' words about the Son of Man sending his angels with a loud trumpet call to gather his elect (Matthew 24:31).
questions: The ancient world feared the sea monster as a threat to order, but the LORD dispatches it in one verse. What forces seem overwhelming to people today, and how does this chapter reframe them?
Compare the vineyard song of 27:2-6 with the one in 5:1-7. What has changed, and what does the change reveal about God?
Verse 9 connects forgiveness with tearing down idols. What would it look like for forgiveness to change what a person actually does with the idols in their own life?
